comparison: Both evaluations support the CRISPR screen methodology and DBT identification (C3, C16-C28). OpenEval emphasizes the convergence of multiple validation approaches, while peer reviewers praised the 'convincing evidence' and 'clean data.' Peer review includes C4 not present in OpenEval result. Both conclude the findings are well-supported.

Perfect alignment on claims C29-C38 regarding reduced ubiquitinated protein accumulation. Both evaluations support the findings using immunoblotting, immunofluorescence, and ProteoStat dye approaches. OpenEval highlights the convergence of multiple assays, while peer reviewers accepted the findings as part of a 'well-designed' mechanistic pathway.

Complete agreement on claims C39-C42 showing that DBT loss does not affect proteasome function. Both evaluations support this negative result as important for ruling out direct proteasome mechanisms. OpenEval emphasizes the well-controlled nature of the experiment, while peer reviewers accepted it without challenge as supporting the autophagy-based mechanism.

Perfect alignment on claims C44-C61 regarding autophagy flux enhancement. Both evaluations strongly support the autophagy mechanism with Bafilomycin A1 experiments. OpenEval emphasizes methodological soundness and convergent evidence, while peer reviewers explicitly endorsed this as a key mechanism with 'convincing evidence' noted in the editor's summary.

Complete agreement on claims C64-C71 regarding BCAA accumulation and pathway blockade. Both evaluations support the conclusion that pathway blockade, not metabolite accumulation, is key. OpenEval praises the experimental design distinguishing alternative hypotheses, while peer reviewers accepted the metabolic mechanism without challenge.

Perfect alignment on claims C72-C78 regarding ATP/ADP ratios and energy status. Both evaluations support the energetic mechanism with bidirectional glucose manipulation experiments. OpenEval emphasizes the causal role established by dose-dependent effects, while peer reviewers integrated this into the accepted mechanistic pathway.

Complete agreement on claims C80-C88 regarding AMPK activation. Both evaluations strongly support AMPK as a key mechanistic node using genetic and pharmacological approaches. OpenEval highlights convergence of loss- and gain-of-function experiments, while peer reviewers explicitly noted AMPK and downstream signaling as 'well-justified' conclusions.

Strong alignment on ULK1 phosphorylation claims (C90-C91, C94-C98). OpenEval covers both ULK1 and TSC2 phosphorylation (C94-C103), while peer review focuses on ULK1 as part of the AMPK downstream pathway. Both support the autophagy activation mechanism, with peer reviewers praising the 'careful delineation' of the pathway.

Substantial overlap on mTOR pathway claims (C104-C109 in both). OpenEval emphasizes TSC1 knockdown and bidirectional pharmacological validation, while peer review focuses on mTOR as downstream of AMPK (includes C101-C103). Both strongly support the mTOR-autophagy connection with convergent genetic and pharmacological evidence.

Perfect alignment on claims C112-C122 regarding TDP-43 protection across cell types and model systems. Both evaluations support the mechanistic findings in RPE1 cells and motor neurons. OpenEval emphasizes protein turnover kinetics, while peer reviewers highlighted the implications for ALS/FTD pathogenesis. Both note strong cross-validation.

Complete agreement on claims C123-C125 regarding Drosophila validation. Both evaluations support the in vivo findings using RNAi and CRISPR approaches. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of two genetic methods in whole organisms, while peer reviewers explicitly noted the cross-species validation and eye phenotype rescue.

Perfect alignment on claims C126-C131 regarding polyQ protection. Both evaluations support the broad-spectrum nature of DBT's protective effects beyond TDP-43. OpenEval highlights validation across mammalian and Drosophila systems, while peer reviewers explicitly mentioned both polyglutamine and TDP-43 models as evidence of generalizability.

Complete agreement on claims C132-C136 regarding elevated DBT in ALS patient tissues. Both evaluations support the clinical relevance using immunoblotting and immunofluorescence. OpenEval notes the data establish correlation rather than causation, while peer reviewers emphasized translational implications for ALS/FTD pathogenesis.

Strong alignment on overarching conclusions (C10, C137-C138). Both evaluations support DBT as a master regulator with therapeutic implications. OpenEval includes additional mechanistic model claims (C142-C143) and covers more background claims. Peer reviewers emphasized the novel discovery and pathogenic relevance, while OpenEval provides more detailed mechanistic justification.
